In numerical differentiation known function values are used to find approximations to the derivative.
In *numerical integration* the same information is used to find approximations to the *integral*. These methods are useful when the function is only known at isolated points, or when it is difficult or impossible to compute the integral by hand.

In @sec-differentiation we explained a general algorithm for deriving methods of numerical differentiation.
The corresponding algorithm for numerical integration is as follows:

* Find the polynomial interpolating the function in a suitable set of points, 
* use the integral of this polynomial as an approximation to the integral of the function.
* analyse the truncation error in a way similar to that of numerical differentiation.

We start this chapter by revisiting the definition of the integral (@sec-defint).
Then we look at the simplest method for numerical integration, the midpoint method (@sec-midpoint).
In @sec-othermethods we will then formulate the general algorithm stated above in more detail, and look at some important special cases.


## Definition of the integral {#sec-defint}
The integral of a function $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ is interpreted as the area under the graph, where the positive values of $f$ 
have a positive contribution to the area, and the negative values have a negative contribution (see @fig-integralarea). 
The standard notation for the integral is
$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, dx.
$$
Before we continue we must introduce a concept which we will use several times in our definition of the integral.

![The area under the graph of a function.](integralarea.pdf){#fig-integralarea}

::: {#def- name='Partition'}
Let $a$ and $b$ be two real numbers with $a<b$. A *partition* of $[a,b]$ is a collection of numbers $\{x_0,x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ so that
$$
a=x_0<x_1<x_2\cdots<x_{n-1}<x_n=b.
$$
The partition is said to be *uniform* if $x_i-x_{i-1}=(b-a)/n$ for $i=1$, \dots, $n$. 
The distance between the points, $h=(b-a)/n$, is then called the *step length* of the partition.
:::

If $\Pi=\{x_0,x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ is a partition, we let the *size* of the partition be $|\Pi| = \max_{i=1,\dots,n}|x_i-x_{i-1}|$, 
i.e. the largest distance between neighbouring points. If $\Pi$ is uniform, $|\Pi|=(b-a)/n$.


To define the integral one uses so-called *Riemann sums*, which are approximations to the area under the graph.
We choose a partition $\Pi = \{x_0,x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ of $[a,b]$, and find the maximum and minimum of $f$ on each sub-interval 
$[x_{i-1},x_i]$,
$$
m_i=\min_{x\in[x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x), \qquad M_i=\max_{x\in[x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x) \qquad \text{for } i=1,2,\dots,n.
$$
The min and the max here may or may not exist. Continuity of $f$ will secure this, however. 
Approximations to the integral can be obtained from two different piecewise constant functions, 
both being constant on each sub-interval $[x_{i-1},x_i)$:
The first equals $m_i$ on this sub-interval, the second equals $M_i$ (see @fig-integraldef). 
We sum up the areas under the two, and end up with the two approximations
$$
\underline{I}(\Pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i(x_i-x_{i-1}), \qquad \overline{I}(\Pi)=\sum_{i=1}^n M_i (x_i-x_{i-1}).
$$ {#eq-ulstepdef}
The first approximation is in general too small, the second too large. 
The integral is obtained by letting the size of the partition go to zero. 


::: {#fig-integraldef layout-ncol=2}

![](integrallower1.pdf)
![](integrallower2.pdf)

![](integralupper1.pdf)
![](integralupper2.pdf)

Inscribed (left) and circumscribed (right) piecewise constant functions for a partition (top) and a finer partition (bottom).
:::

::: {#def-integral name='The integral'}
Let $f$ be a function defined on the interval $[a,b]$. If 
$$
\sup_{\Pi}\underline{I}(\Pi) \text{ and } \inf_{\Pi} \overline{I}(\Pi)
$$
exist (where the infimum and supremum are taken over all partitions of $[a,b]$) and are equal, we say that $f$ is *integrable*, 
and we define the integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$,  $\int_a^b f(x)\, dx$, as the common value of the two. 
:::

The construction of the integral is illustrated @fig-integraldef, 
where we see how the piecewise constant approximations become better as the partitions get finer.
It turns out that the following holds

::: {#thm-contintg}
Any continuous function is integrable. 
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $\Pi_n=\{x_0,\dots,x_n\}$ be partitions of $[a,b]$ so that the size of the partitions go to 0, the size of a partition being 
the largest distance between neighbouring points $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i$. We have that 
$$\underline{I}(\Pi_n)\leq  \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \leq \overline{I}(\Pi_n).$$ {#eq-help2prove}
Assume that $\epsilon$ is given. 
Since $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, it is also uniformly continuous on $[a,b]$. 
Due to this, and since the size of the partitions goes to 0, 
there exists an $N$ so that, for $n\geq N$, $|f(x)-f(y)|\leq\epsilon/(b-a)$ for $x,y$ in the same sub-interval of $\Pi_n$. 
In particular this means that $M_i-m_i\leq \epsilon/(b-a)$, and we get
$$\overline{I}(\Pi_n)-\underline{I}(\Pi_n)=\sum_{i=1}^n (M_i-m_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})\leq \frac{\epsilon}{b-a}(x_i-x_{i-1})=\frac{\epsilon}{b-a}(b-a)=\epsilon.$$ 
The result now follows from @eq-help2prove.
:::

The integral has a property which is very useful when it comes to numerical computation:

::: {#thm-fundnumint}
Let $f\colon [a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous, let $\Pi_n=\{x_0,\dots,x_n\}$ be a partition of $[a,b]$, and let $t_i$ be a number in $[x_{i-1},x_i]$ for every $i=1$, \dots, $n$. Then the sum
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})
$$ {#eq-fundnumint}
will converge to $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ as the "size" of the $\Pi_n$ goes to 0.
:::

Thus, in general we can derive methods for numerical integration by splitting $[a,b]$ in small sub-intervals, 
and add together contributions from each sub-interval. 

::: {.proof}
We have that 
$$\underline{I}(\Pi_n) \leq \sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i)(x_i-x_{i-1}) \leq \overline{I}(\Pi_n)$$
The result follows by combining this with @eq-help2prove.
:::


Different choices for the $t_i$ in @thm-fundnumint give rise to various methods for approximating the integral.
We could for instance choose $t_i$ as the maximum or the minimum on each sub-interval,
but the problem with this is that it can be both hard and time-consuming to find maxima and minima, even for a computer.
We could also choose $t_i$ equal to one of the end points $x_{i-1}$ or $x_i$, but it turns out that better choices exist, 
as we will see.


## The midpoint method {#sec-midpoint}
An even better choice for the $t_i$ turns out to be the midpoint $t_i=(x_i+x_{i-1})/2$ on each sub-interval.
With this choice @eq-fundnumint gives the approximation
$$
I\approx \sum_{i=1}^n f\bigl((x_i+x_{i-1})/2\bigr)(x_i-x_{i-1}).
$$ {#eq-midpointint}

::: {#def- name='The midpoint method'}
Let $f$ be a function which is integrable on the interval $[a,b]$, and let $\{x_i\}_{i=0}^n$ be a partition of $[a,b]$.
The *midpoint method* approximates the integral of $f$ with
$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, dx\approx I_\text{mid}(h)=h\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_{i-1/2}),
$$ {#eq-midpointdef}
where $x_{i-1/2}=(x_{i-1}+x_i)/2=a+(i-1/2)h$.
:::

We can think of this as a constant approximation on each sub-interval, where the constant is the value in the midpoint. 
The method is illustrated in @fig-midpoint for the cases with one and five sub-intervals.

::: {#fig-midpoint layout-ncol=2}

![](midapp1.pdf){#fig-midapp1}

![](midapp5.pdf){#fig-midapp5}

The midpoint method with one sub-interval (@fig-midapp1), and five sub-intervals (@fig-midapp5)}.
:::

The midpoint method gives only an approximation, and will produce a small error. 
As in @sec-differentiation we shall estimate how large this error can be. 
This can be done in two steps. First we analyse the error in the case of only one sub-interval. This is called the *local error*.
Then we find an estimate for the general case with many sub-intervals. This is called the *global error*.


### The local error
The error in the midpoint method with one sub-interval only is
$$
E = \int_a^b f(x)\, dx-f(m)(b-a),
$$ {#eq-midpointerr}
where $m=(a+b)/2$. If we use a Taylor expansion of $f$ around the midpoint $m$ we get
$$
f(x)=f(m)+(x-m)f'(m)+\frac{(x-m)^2}{2}f''(\xi),\\
$$
where $\xi$ is a number between $m$ and $x$, which depends on $x$. Integrating this we get
\begin{align*}
\int_a^b f(x)\, dx&=\int_a^b\Bigl(f(m)+(x-m)f'(m)+\frac{(x-m)^2}{2}f''(\xi)\Bigr)\, dx\\
    &=f(m)(b-a)+\frac{f'(m)}{2}\bigl[(x-m)^2\bigr]_a^b+\frac{1}{2}\int_a^b (x-m)^2 f''(\xi)\, dx\\
    &=f(m)(b-a)+\frac{1}{2}\int_a^b (x-m)^2 f''(\xi)\, dx,
\end{align*}
where the term in the middle was $0$. This leads us to the expression
$$
|E| = \left|\int_a^b f(x)\, dx-f(m)(b-a)\right|=\frac{1}{2}\left|\int_a^b (x-m)^2 f''(\xi)\, dx\right|.
$$
Some more calculations give
\begin{align*}
|E| &= \frac{1}{2}\left|\int_a^b(x-m)^2 f''(\xi)\, dx\right| \le \frac{1}{2}\int_a^b\left| (x-m)^2 f''(\xi)\right|\, dx\\
&= \frac{1}{2}\int_a^b (x-m)^2 \left|f''(\xi)\right|\, dx\\
 &\le \frac{M_2}{2}\int_a^b(x-m)^2\, dx\\[3pt]
 &=\frac{M_2}{2}\frac{1}{3}\left[(x-m)^3\right]_a^b\\[3pt]
 &=\frac{M_2}{6}\bigl((b-m)^3-(a-m)^3\bigr)\\
 &=\frac{M_2}{24}(b-a)^3,
\end{align*}
where $M_2=\max_{x\in[a,b]}\bigl| f''(x)\bigr|$.
The inequality on the first line holds because, when we move the absolute value inside the integral, the function we integrate becomes non-negative everywhere.
This means that areas where the integrand originally was negative, now become positive, so that the second integral is larger than the first.

The equality on the second line holds since $(x-m)^2$ is never negative, and the inequality on the third line holds since we replace $\left|f''(\xi)\right|$ with its maximum on the interval $[a,b]$.
On the fourth line we simply compute the integral of $(x-m)^2$. Then we insert the limits. The last line follows from that $(b-m)^3=-(a-m)^3=(b-a)^3/8$.
We have thus proved the following lemma.

::: {#lem-midpointlocalerr}
Let $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function, with continuous first- and second order derivatives. The error in the midpoint method with one sub-interval is then bounded by
$$
\left|\int_a^b f(x)\, dx-f(m)(b-a)\right|\le\frac{M_2}{24}(b-a)^3,
$$
where $m=(a+b)/2$.
:::

The important thing in @lem-midpointlocalerr is the factor $(b-a)^3$.
This implies that, if we halve the with of the intervals, the error in the method will be reduced with a factor of $8$.




### The global error
Let us now see consider the error resulting from adding together contributions from many sub-intervals. 
$[a,b]$ is partitioned into $n$ sub-intervals, all with width $h=(b-a)/n$. With
\begin{align*}
I&=\int_a^b f(x)\, dx=\sum_{i=1}^n \int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} f(x)\, dx, & I_\text{mid}(h)&=\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_{i-1/2})h,
\end{align*}
the total error in the midpoint method is
$$
I-I_\text{mid}(h)=\sum_{i=1}^n \Biggl(\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} f(x)\, dx-f(x_{i-1/2})h\Biggr),
$$
where the expression inside the parenthesis is the local error on the interval $[x_{i-1},x_i]$. We therefore have
$$
\begin{split}
\left|I-I_\text{mid}(h)\right|&=\left|\sum_{i=1}^n \left(\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} f(x)\, dx-f(x_{i-1/2})h\right)\right|\notag\\
&\le \sum_{i=1}^n\left|\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} f(x)\, dx-f(x_{i-1/2})h\right|\notag\\
&\le \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{h^3}{24}M_2^{(i)}
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-localsum}
where $M_2^{(i)} = \max_{x\in[x_{i-1},x_i]} \bigl|f''(x)\bigr|$. In the first inequality the triangle inequality was applied, while we in the second inequality have used @lem-midpointlocalerr.
We can simplify @eq-localsum further by using the maximum over the entire $[a,b]$, instead of over $[x_{i-1},x_i]$: For all $i$ we have that
$$
M_2^{(i)}=\max_{x\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}\left|f''(x)\right|\le \max_{x\in[a,b]}\left|f''(x)\right|=M_2,
$$
so that @eq-localsum simplifies to
$$
|I-I_\text{mid}(h)| \leq \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{h^3}{24}M^{(i)}\le \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{h^3}{24}M_2=\frac{h^3}{24}nM_2.
$$ {#eq-globalstep}
Since $h=(b-a)/n$, we get $hn=b-a$. Inserting this in @eq-globalstep, we get the following estimate for the global error.

::: {#thm-midgloberr}
Suppose that $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ and its first two derivatives are continuous. Then the error in the midpoint method is bounded by
$$
|I-I_\text{mid}(h)| \le (b-a)\frac{h^2}{24}M_2.
$$ {#eq-midpointglobalerr}
:::



### The step length
We want to approximate the integral, and let us say we want the error in the approximation to be smaller than some $\epsilon>0$. We can use the error estimate in @eq-midpointglobalerr by requiring that
$$
(b-a)\frac{h^2}{24}\max_{x\in[a,b]}M_2 \le \epsilon
$$
which easily can be solved for $h$,
$$
h\le\sqrt{\frac{24\epsilon}{(b-a)M_2}}.
$$
If we can compute or estimate $M_2$, the maximal value of the second derivative, we can insert this in the expression above, and find an upper bound for $h$ which guarantees the error in the integral becomes less than $\epsilon$.




## General method for deriving numerical integration methods {#sec-othermethods}
There also exist many other methods for numerical integration. 
The following algorithm for deriving approximations to $I=\int_a^b f(x)\, dx$ is a direct parallel to that of numerical differentiation. 

1. Let $n,k\geq 1$. Split the interval $[a,b]$ into $nk$ equally large sub-intervals
$$
a=x_0<x_1<x_2<\cdots < x_{nk-1}<x_{nk}=b.
$$
Set $h=(b-a)/n$.
2. For each sub-interval $J_i=[x_{(i-1)k},x_{ik}]$, find the polynomial $p_{k,i}$ of degree $k$ which interpolates $f$ in the $k+1$ points $\bigl\{x_{(i-1)k},\dots,x_{ik}\bigr\}$.
3. Use $\int_{J_i} p_{k,i}(x)\,dx$ as an approximation to $\int_{J_i} f(x)\,dx$, and add these together to obtain
$$
I(h) = \sum_{i=1}^n \int_{J_i} p_{k,i}(x)\,dx.
$$

This algorithm is also called the *Newton--Cotes method*. With help of the analysis in @sec-app we can estimate the error in this method:

::: {#thm-}
Let $n,k\geq 1$ and let $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function with $k+1$ continuous derivatives. Then the error in the Newton--Cotes method of order $k$ with step length $h=(b-a)/n$ satisfies
$$
|I-I(h)| \leq \frac{(b-a)M_{k+1}}{(k+1)!} h^{k+1}.
$$ {#eq-newton-cotes-feil}

:::

::: {.proof}
Choose a sub-interval $J_i$, and let $p_{k,i}$ be the polynomial of degree $\leq k$ interpolating $f$ in the points $x_{ik},\dots,x_{(i+1)k}$ (as describes in the general algorithm of numerical integration). From @thm-interpolasjonsfeil we know that for $x\in J_i$
$$
|f(x)-p_{k,i}(x)| \leq \frac{M_{k+1}}{(k+1)!}\bigl(x_{(i+1)k}-x_{ik}\bigr)^{k+1} = \frac{M_{k+1}}{(k+1)!}h^{k+1}.
$$
Therefore
\begin{align*}
|I-I(h)| &= \Biggl|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx - \sum_{i=1}^n \int_{J_i} p_{k,i}(x)\,dx\Biggr|
= \Biggl|\sum_{i=1}^n \int_{J_i} f(x)-p_{k,i}(x)\,dx\Biggr| \\
&\leq \sum_{i=1}^n \int_{J_i} |f(x)-p_{k,i}(x)|\,dx \\
&\leq \sum_{i=1}^n \int_{J_i} \frac{M_{k+1}}{(k+1)!}h^{k+1}\,dx \\
&= \frac{M_{k+1}}{(k+1)!}\sum_{i=1}^n h^{k+2} \\
&= \frac{M_{k+1}}{(k+1)!}nh^{k+2}.
\end{align*}
(From the first to the second line we use the triangle inequality, then we inserted the error estimate for the interpolant, and then we integrated the constant $M_{k+1}/(k+1)!h^{k+1}$.)
If we now insert $h=(b-a)/n$ we get @eq-newton-cotes-feil.
:::

From the error estimate @eq-newton-cotes-feil we see that, to decrease the error, we can increase $k$, decrease $h$ (i.e., increasing $n$), or a combination of the two. 
What combination is the most effective depends on how large the factor $M_{k+1}$ is for different $k$. 

In the next sections we will consider the cases $k=1$, which gives the trapezoidal rule, 
and the case $k=2$, which gives Simpson's method. 

## The trapezoidal rule
We know that the line which interpolates $f$ in the two points $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i$ is
$$
p_{1,i}(x)=f(x_{i-1}) + \frac{f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})}{x_i-x_{i-1}}(x-x_{i-1}).
$$
If we apply this in the general algorithm we get *the trapezoidal rule*; as we see from @fig-trapezoiddef the approximation in each sub-interval $J_i$ is a trapezoid. 
We then get the approximation
$$
\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} p_{1,i}(x)\,dx= \frac{f(x_{i-1})+f(x_i)}{2}h.
$$
Adding the contributions from all sub-intervals we get the approximation
$$
I_\text{trap}(h)=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f(x_{i-1})+f(x_i)}{2}h.
$$
Since $x_i$ is both the end of one interval and the beginning of the next for $i\neq 0,n$, this can be written as
$$
I_\text{trap}(h)=h\left(  \frac{f(a)+f(b)}{2} + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f(x_i) \right).
$$ {#eq-trapezoid0}




::: {#fig-trapezoiddef layout-ncol=2}

![](trapapp1.pdf){#fig-trapapp1}

![](trapapp5.pdf){#fig-trapapp5}

The trapezoidal rule with one sub-interval (@fig-trapapp1), and 5 sub-intervals (@fig-trapapp5)}.
:::


If we apply @thm-interpolasjonsfeil with $k=1$ we get the following error estimate.

::: {#thm- name='Error estimate for the trapezoidal rule'}
Let $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be a two times continuously differentiable function. The error in the trapezoidal rule with step length $h$ is then bounded by
$$
|I-I_\text{trap}(h)| \le \frac{(b-a)M_2}{2}h^2.
$$ {#eq-trapglobalerr}
:::


With some more computation one can show that  the trapezoidal rule has an error at most $\frac{(b-a)M_2}{12}h^2$, i.e., six times lower than the right hand side in @eq-trapglobalerr
(see @exr-trapezoidal_estimate). The error estimate given by @eq-trapglobalerr is thus an *over-estimate*. The constant factor $\frac16$ is not particularly important; the important thing in @eq-trapglobalerr is

* the factor $h^2$, which means that if we for instance halve $h$, the error will be reduced by a factor of $1/4$.
* the factor $M_2$, i.e., the error estimate depends on the seconds derivative.

An implementation of the trapezoidal rule can be as follows.

## Simpson's method
For $k=2$ we approximate with a quadratic polynomial on each sub-interval $J_i$.
The method in this case is called *Simpson's method*, and is illustrated in @fig-simpdef.

::: {#fig-simpdef layout-ncol=2}

![](simpapp1.pdf){#fig-simpapp1}

![](simpapp3.pdf){#fig-simpapp3}

Simpson's method with one sub-interval (@fig-simpapp1), and three sub-intervals (@fig-simpapp3)}.
:::

In @exr-simpson you will be asked to show that the Newton form of the polynomial interpolating 
$f$ in $a$, $m=(a+b)/2$, and $b$ is
$$p_2(x)=f(a) + \frac{f(m)-f(a)}{h}(x-a) + \frac{f(a) - 2f(m)+f(b)}{2h^2}(x-a)(x-m),$$
where $h=(b-a)/2$, and that
$$\int_a^b p_2(x)\,dx = \frac{h}{3}  \left(  f(a) + 4f(m) + f(b) \right).$$
This is Simpson's method with one sub-interval. If we add together contributions from all sub-intervals we get
$$
I_\text{Simp}(h)=\frac{h}{3} \Biggl(f(a)+f(b)+2 \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f(x_{2i}) + 4\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_{2i-1})\Biggr),
$$ {#eq-simpsonssum}
where now $h=(b-a)/(2n)$
If we insert $k=2$ in @thm-interpolasjonsfeil, we get the following error estimate for this method.


::: {#thm- name="Error estimate for Simpson's method"}
Let $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be a four times continuously differentiable function. The error in Simpson's method 
with step length $h$ is then bounded by
$$|I-I_\text{Simp}(h)| \le \frac{(b-a)M_3}{6}h^3.$$ {#eq-simpglobalerr}
:::

Simpson's method is much used. Since it is based on quadratic polynomials, it must be exact for such polynomials.
It is in fact exact for all cubic polynomials also (see @exr-simpson_exact_third).
There are sharper error estimates for Simpson's method than this (see @exr-proofsimpson, 
which goes a bit outside the curriculum). 

An implementation of Simpson's method can be as follows

In @tbl-intmethods we have listed errors in the approximations to $\int_0^1 \cos\,dx=\sin 1\approx0.8414709848$ 
obtained by the three methods we have considered. 
The interval $[0,1]$ has been split into $2^k$ sub-intervals of equal length, for $k=1$, $2$, \dots, 10, 


::: {#tbl-intmethods}
```{python}
#| echo: false
a, b = 0, 1
f = np.cos
exact = np.sin(1)
nvals = 2**(np.arange(1,11))
approx1 = [midpointn(f, a, b, n) for n in nvals] 
approx2 = [trapezoidaln(f, a, b, n) for n in nvals] 
approx3 = [simpsonn(f, a, b, n) for n in nvals] 
df = pd.DataFrame({
          'n': nvals,
          'Midpoint': np.abs(exact - approx1),
          'Trapezoidal': np.abs(exact - approx2),
          'Simpson': np.abs(exact - approx3)})
df.index=[''] *len(df)
df
```
Truncation errors for three of the methods we have considered, for different numbers of sub-intervals. 
:::


Each time $h$ is halved we see that

* For the midpoint method the error is reduced about a factor of $4$. This confirms what we derived in in @thm-midgloberr.
* For the trapezoidal rule the error is also reduced about a factor of 4, but the error is actually twice as big when compared to the midpoint method (even if we now use two function values in each sub-interval to estimate the integral!). 
This can also be seen from the error estimate in @eq-trapglobalerr, since $1/12$ is twice as big as $1/24$ in @eq-midpointglobalerr. 
* For Simpson's method, the error is reduced by a factor of about $16$.

## Reducing the step length in the midpoint method.

When reducing the step length $h$ in the midpoint method with a factor of 3, the error is reduced by a factor of about 9.

## Midpoint method with two sub-intervals.

We use the midpoint method with two subintervals to find an approximation to the integral
$$
\int_0^1 x^2 \, dx.
$$
What do we get?

> $I_\text{mid} = \frac{1}{2}f(1/4) + \frac{1}{2}f(3/4) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{16} + \frac{1}{2}\frac{9}{16} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{10}{16} = \frac{5}{16}$.

## Comparison of errors in the midpoint method and the trapezoidal rule.

The trapezoidal rule is usually more accurate than the midpoint method.

> The midpoint method has an error bounded by $(b-a)h^2M_2/24$, while the best estimate we found for the trapezoidal rule was $(b-a)h^2M_2/12$.

## Function evaluations for the trapezoidal rule.

Since every evaluation point in the trapezoidal rule occurs as the end point in two different sub-intervals, 
we must evaluate the function we integrate twice in every point. 

> Instead of computing the same function value $f(x_i)$ twice we can write $2f(x_i)$, since everything will be summed together.

Simpson's method requires us to use an odd number of points.

> For an interval three partition points are needed. For every interval we add two more partition points, so that the total number of point always is odd.

Simpson's method is exact for polynomials of degree three or lower.

::: {#exr-}
In this exercise we will use the definition of the integral on the function $f(x)=e^{x}$ on the interval $[0,1]$.

(a) Write and run a program that computes $\underline{I}$ and $\overline{I}$ for a uniform partition of 10 sub-intervals 
(let the method take take the number of sub-intervals as argument). 
What is the error from the exact value $I=e-1 = 1.718281828$ of the integral?

::::: {.callout-tip title='Hint' collapse="true"}
Instead of a `for`-loop here you can use the `sum`-command when you add together the contribution from the sub-intervals.
:::::

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
On each sub-interval $f$ assumes its smallest value in the left end point, its largest value in the right end point. 
Here we can use the `sum`-command the following way to find $\underline{I}(\Pi)$ and $\overline{I}(\Pi)$. 

```{python}
#| lst-cap: "Computation of the upper/lower-integral"
# pyodide: autorun
def int_vals(n):
    l = (1/n)*np.sum(np.exp(   np.arange(0,n)/n ))
    u = (1/n)*np.sum(np.exp( np.arange(1,n+1)/n ))
    l_err = np.abs(l-(np.exp(1)-1))
    u_err = np.abs(u-(np.exp(1)-1))
    return l,u,l_err,u_err
```

Running the code you get 
```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
l,u,l_err,u_err=int_vals(10)
print(l,u,l_err,u_err)
```

:::::::
:::::


(b) Write a program which finds how many sub-intervals that are needed to compute $\underline{I}$ with an error less than 
$3\times 10^{-3}$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
We run the following code
```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
n = 1
l,u,l_err,u_err=int_vals(n)
while l_err > 3*10**(-3):
    n += 1
    l,u,l_err,u_err = int_vals(n)
print(n)
```

::: {#exr-sinmidpoint}
Find an approximation to
$$
\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{1+x^{2}}\,dx=0.526978557614\ldots
$$
using the midpoint method with 6 sub-intervals.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
The interval $[0,\pi/2]$ is here split into the intervals
\begin{multline*}
[0,\pi/12], \ [\pi/12,2\pi/12], \ [2\pi/12,3\pi/12], \ [3\pi/12,4\pi/12],\\
[4\pi/12,5\pi/12],\ [5\pi/12,6\pi/12].
\end{multline*}
The midpoints on these intervals are $\pi/24$, $3\pi/24$, $5\pi/24$, $7\pi/24$, $9\pi/24$, $11\pi/24$. 
With $h=\pi/12$ the midpoint method gives
\begin{align*}
I_\text{mid} &= \frac{\pi}{12}\left( f(\pi/24) + f(3\pi/24) + f(5\pi/24) + f(7\pi/24) + f(9\pi/24) + f(11\pi/24) \right) \\
&=
\frac{\pi}{12}\left(\frac{\sin(\pi/24)}{1+(\pi/24)^2}+\frac{\sin(3\pi/24)}{1+(3\pi/24)^2}+\frac{\sin(5\pi/24)}{1+(5\pi/24)^2}+\frac{\sin(7\pi/24)}{1+(7\pi/24)^2}\right.\\
&\left.+\frac{\sin(9\pi/24)}{1+(9\pi/24)^2}+\frac{\sin(11\pi/24)}{1+(11\pi/24)^2}\right)\\
&\approx 0.530624.
\end{align*}
:::::::
:::::
:::

(b) Find a value $h$ which guarantees that the absolute error is less than $10^{-10}$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
From @thm-midgloberr we know that the error is bounded by 
$(b-a)\frac{h^2}{24}\max_{x\in[a,b]}\left|f''(x)\right|$. Since $f''(x)=e^x$,
$\max_{x\in[0,1]}\left|f''(x)\right|=e$, so that this is $\frac{eh^2}{24}$. We therefore must have that $\frac{eh^2}{24}<10^{-10}$, so that
$h<\sqrt{\frac{24}{e}}10^{-5}\approx 2.97\times 10^{-5}$.
:::::::
:::::
:::

::: {#exr-}
How many function evaluations are needed to compute the integral
$$\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+2x}$$
with error less than $10^{-10}$ for

(a) the trapezoidal rule,

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Since the error in the trapezoidal rule is bounded by
$$(b-a)\frac{h^2}{12}\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f''(x)|,$$
and since
$f''(x)=\frac{8}{(1+2x)^3}$ (which has maximum absolute value for $x=0$), we need to choose $h$ so that
$$
(b-a)\frac{h^2}{12}\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f''(x)| = 8\frac{h^2}{12} \leq10^{-10},
$$
which gives that $h\leq 10^{-5}\sqrt{3/2}$. The number of function evaluations is then
$\approx 1/h=10^5/\sqrt{2/3}\approx 81649.66$, which means that at least $81650$ evaluations are needed.
:::::::
:::::

(b) The midpoint method,

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Since the error in the midpoint method is bounded by
$$(b-a)\frac{h^2}{24}\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f''(x)|,$$
we get as in (a) that
$$
(b-a)\frac{h^2}{24}\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f''(x)| = 2\frac{h^2}{6} \leq10^{-10},
$$
which gives that $h\leq 10^{-5}\sqrt{3}$. The number of function evaluations is thus
about $1/h=10^5/\sqrt{3}\approx 57735.03$. In other words, at least $57736$ evaluations are needed.
:::::::
:::::

(c) and Simpson's method?

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Since the error in Simpson's method is bounded by
$$(b-a)\frac{h^4}{180}\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f^{(iv)}(x)|,$$
and since
$f^{(iv)}(x)=\frac{384}{(1+2x)^5}$ (which has maximum absolute value for $x=0$), we need to choose $h$ so that
$$
(b-a)\frac{h^4}{180}\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f^{(iv)}(x)| = 384\frac{h^4}{180} \leq 10^{-10},
$$
which means that $h$ is bounded by $h\leq (180\cdot 10^{-10}/384)^{1/4}$. The number of function evaluations is then
$\approx 1/h=(180\cdot 10^{-10}/384)^{-1/4}\approx 382.17$, which means that at least $383$ evaluations are needed.
:::::::
:::::
:::

::: {#exr-}
We want to write a method for numerical integration on the form
$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, dx \approx w_1 f(a) + w_2 f((a+b)/2)+w_3 f(b),
$$
where the $w_i$ are to be decided.
Show that, if the method is exact for the three polynomials $f(x)=x^i$ for $i=0,1,2$, then the method coincides with Simpson's method.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Since $\int_a^b f(x)\, dx = w_1 f(a) + w_2 f((a+b)/2)+w_3 f(b)$ for $f(x)=x^i$ for $i=0,1,2$, then this also holds for the polynomial $p_2$ which interpolates $f$ in $a$, $(a+b)/2$, and $b$.
We therefore get
$$\int_a^b p_2(x)\, dx = w_1 p_2(a) + w_2 p_2((a+b)/2)+w_3 p_2(b) = w_1 f(a) + w_2 f((a+b)/2)+w_3 f(b).$$
We have also shown that the first equals
$\frac{b-a}{6}(f(a) + 4f((a+b)/2) + f(b))$, so that
$$
w_1 f(a) + w_2 f((a+b)/2)+w_3 f(b) = \frac{b-a}{6}(f(a) + 4f((a+b)/2) + f(b)).
$$
By setting $f(a)=1$, $f((a+b)/2)=f(b)=0$ we see that $w_1=\frac{b-a}{6}$, and similarly for $w_2$, $w_3$.
It follows that the method coincides with Simpson's method.
:::::::
:::::
:::




::: {#exr-trapezoidal_estimate}
Let $m=\frac{a+b}{2}$ be the midpoint of the interval $[a,b]$, and consider the following application of integration by parts:
\begin{align*}
-\int_a^b (x-m)f'(x)\,dx &= -\left[ (x-m)f(x)  \right]_a^b + \int_a^b f(x)\,dx  \\
&= -\frac{b-a}{2}f(b) - \frac{b-a}{2}f(a) + \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \\
&= \int_a^b f(x)\,dx - (b-a) \frac{f(a)+f(b)}{2}.
\end{align*}
This shows that the local error in the trapezoidal rule can be written as
$$ L=-\int_a^b (x-m)f'(x)\,dx.$$ {#eq-expr:locerr}

(a) Apply integration by parts to @eq-expr:locerr to show that
$$L = \int_a^b \left( C +\frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2 \right) f''(x)\,dx.$$ {#eq-locerr2}
where $C$ is a constant (we will get back to how we can choose $C$).

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Integration by parts on @eq-expr:locerr with constant $C$ in the anti-derivative of $x-m$ gives
\begin{align*}
L &= - \left[  \left( C +\frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2 \right) f'(x)\right]_a^b + \int_a^b \left( C +\frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2 \right) f''(x)\,dx \\
   &= \int_a^b \left( C +\frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2 \right) f''(x)\,dx.
\end{align*}
which shows @eq-locerr2.
:::::::
:::::

(b) Show that, with $C=-(b-a)^2/8$, we have that $C +\frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2\leq 0$ for $x\in[a,b]$.
Show also that, with this choice of $C$, it follows from @eq-locerr2 that $|L|\leq\frac{M_2(b-a)^3}{12}$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
For $x\in[a,b]$ we have that $\frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2\leq \frac{1}{8}(b-a)^2=-C$, so that $-C -\frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2\geq 0$ for such $x$.
Taking absolute values in @eq-locerr2 with this choice of $C$ gives
\begin{align*}
|L| &= \left|   \int_a^b \left( \frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2 - (b-a)^2/8\right) f''(x)\,dx   \right| \\
&\leq \int_a^b \left| \frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2 - (b-a)^2/8\right| |f''(x)|\,dx \\
&\leq \int_a^b \left( (b-a)^2/8 - \frac{1}{2}(x-m)^2 \right) M_2\,dx \\
&= M_2 \left[  x(b-a)^2/8 - \frac{1}{6}(x-m)^3 \right]_a^b \\
&= M_2\left( (b-a)^3/8 - \frac{1}{48} (b-a)^3 - \frac{1}{48} (b-a)^3\right) \\
&= M_2\left( \frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{24}\right)(b-a)^3 = \frac{M_2(b-a)^3}{12}.
\end{align*}
:::::::
:::::

(c) Use (b) to show that the global error in the trapezoidal rule is $\leq (b-a) \frac{h^2}{12}M_2$. 

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
As for the midpoint method we get the global error by summing the local errors (replace $b-a$ with $h$, and $nh$ with $b-a$):
$$\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{M_2h^3}{12} = n\frac{M_2h^3}{12} = (b-a) \frac{h^2}{12}M_2.$$
This is what we needed to show.
:::::::
:::::
:::

To simplify notation in the next exercises we define $m=a+h$, and $b=a+2h$. We also define
$$q(x)=(x-a)(x-m)(x-b),$$
and $p_2(x)$ as the quadratic polynomial interpolating $f$ in $a$, $m$, and $b$.



::: {#exr-simpson_exact_third}
In this exercise we will look at different ways of proving that Simpson's method is exact for all cubic polynomials.

(a) Verify that Simpson's method is exact for $f(x)=x^i$ for $i=0$, 1, 2, 3.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
It is enough to verify that Simpson's method is exact on each sub-interval. The integrals become
\begin{align*}
\int_{a-h}^{a+h} x^3dx &= \frac{1}{4}((a+h)^4-(a-h)^4) = 2a^3h + 2ah^3 \\
\int_{a-h}^{a+h} x^2dx &= \frac{1}{3}((a+h)^3-(a-h)^3) = \frac{1}{3}(6a^2h+2h^3) = \frac{h}{3}(6a^2+2h^2)\\
\int_{a-h}^{a+h} xdx   &= \frac{1}{2}((a+h)^2-(a-h)^2) = \frac{1}{2}4ah = 2ah\\
\int_{a-h}^{a+h} dx    &= 2h.
\end{align*}
we also get that the method becomes
\begin{align*}
\frac{h}{3}((a-h)^3+4a^3+(a+h)^3) &= \frac{h}{3}(6a^3 + 6ah^2) = 2a^3h + 2ah^3\\
\frac{h}{3}((a-h)^2+4a^2+(a+h)^2) &= \frac{h}{3}(6a^2 + 2h^2) \\
\frac{h}{3}((a-h)+4a+(a+h)) &= 2ah\\
\frac{h}{3}(1+4+1) &= 2h.
\end{align*}
This shows that Simpson's method is exact for the given polynomials.
:::::::
:::::

(b) Use (a) to show that Simpson's method is exact for any cubic polynomial.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
For $f(x)=bx^3+cx^2+dx+e$ the integral becomes
$$\int_{a-h}^{a+h} f(x)dx = b\int_{a-h}^{a+h} x^3dx+c\int_{a-h}^{a+h} x^2dx+d\int_{a-h}^{a+h} xdx+e\int_{a-h}^{a+h} 1dx.$$
The method now becomes
\begin{align*}
&\frac{h}{3}(f(a-h)+4f(a)+f(a+h))\\
&=b\frac{h}{3}((a-h)^3+4a^3+(a+h)^3)+c\frac{h}{3}((a-h)^2+4a^2+(a+h)^2)\\
&+d\frac{h}{3}((a-h)+4a+(a+h))+e\frac{h}{3}(1+4+1)
\end{align*}
Equality follows now from that we have equality for $x^3$, $x^2$, $x$, and $1$.
:::::::
:::::

(c) Could you come to the same conclusion as in (b) by considering the error estimate given by @eq-simpglobalerr?

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Since $f^{(4)}(x)=0$ for all $x$ for any cubic polynomial, it follows directly from the error estimate that the method is exact for such functions.
:::::::
:::::

(d) Explain that $q$ is anti-symmetric about $m$, and that, if $f$ is a cubic polynomial, then $f-p_2$ is a multiple of $q$.
Why does exactness of Simpson's method for cubic polynomer follow from this?

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
We have that
\begin{align*}
q(m-y) &= (h-y)(-y)(-h-y) \\
q(m+y)&= (h+y)y(-h+y) = -(h-y)(-y)(-h-y),
\end{align*}
so that $q(m-y)=-q(m+y)$. It follows that $q$ is anti-symmetric about $m$, so that $\int_a^b q(x)\,dx =0$.
Suppose now that $f$ is a cubic polynomial. The Newton forms are
\begin{align*}
p_2(x) &= c_0 + c_1(x-a) + c_2(x-a)(x-m) \\
f(x)      &= c_0 + c_1(x-a)  + c_2(x-a)(x-m) + c_3(x-a)(x-m)(x-b)
\end{align*}
Since $\int_a^b (x-a)(x-m)(x-b)\,dx=\int_a^bq(x)\,dx=0$ it follows that $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\int_a^b p_2(x)$,
so that Simpson's method is exact for all cubic polynomer.
:::::::
:::::
:::



::: {#exr-proofsimpson name="A sharper error estimate for Simpson's method"}
In this exercise we will prove a sharper error estimate than @eq-simpglobalerr for Simpson's method. We let
$$E=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx - \int_a^b p_2(x)\,dx$$
be the error in Simpson's method with one sub-interval.

(a) Show that $\int_a^b xq(x)=- \frac{1}{120} (b-a)^5$, and that $(xq(x))^{(4)} = 4!$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Integration by parts three times gives
\begin{align*}
\int_a^b xq(x) &= \int_a^b x(x-a)(x-m)(x-b)\,dx = -\frac{1}{2}\int_a^b (x-a)^2(x-m)(x-b)\,dx \\
&= \frac{1}{6}\int_a^b (x-a)^3(x-b)\,dx \\
&= - \frac{1}{24} \int_a^b (x-a)^4\,dx \\
&= - \frac{1}{120} (b-a)^5,
\end{align*}
which proves the first part. That $(xq(x))^{(4)} = 4!$ follows by using the rule for differentiating a product four times.
:::::::
:::::

(b) Consider the continuous function
$$\phi(x) = f(x)-p_2(x)-kq(x) - \frac{E}{\int_a^b xq(x)\,dx}xq(x),$$
Show that
$$
\phi^{(4)}(x) = f^{(4)}(x) + 120\frac{4!E}{(b-a)^5},
$$ {#eq-phi4der}
and that $\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx=0$. Finally, explain that $\phi(a)=\phi(m)=\phi(b)=0$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
We have that $p_2^{(4)}(x)=q^{(4)}(x)=0$. Insertion of $(xq(x))^{(4)}=4!$, and $\int_a^b xq(x)\,dx=- \frac{1}{120} (b-a)^5$ from (a), proves the first part.
For the second part, we know from before that $\int_a^b q(x)\,dx = 0$.
Integration of $\phi$ from $a$ to $b$ therefore gives
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx - \int_a^b p_2(x)\,dx - E=E-E=0.$$
The last part follows from that $f$ and $p_2$ agree on $a$, $m$, and $b$, and from that $q(a)=q(m)=q(b)=0$.
:::::::
:::::

(c) Show that there exists a $k$ so that $\int_a^m\phi(x)\,dx=0$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
$\int_a^m\phi(x)\,dx=0$ is the same as
$$0 = \int_a^m f(x)\,dx - \int_a^m p_2(x)\,dx- k\int_a^m q(x)\,dx - \frac{E}{\int_a^b xq(x)\,dx}\int_a^m xq(x)\,dx,$$
which can be solved for $k$ by dividing with $\int_a^m q(x)\,dx\neq 0$ (which is $\neq 0$ since $q$ does not how a sign change on $(a,m)$).
:::::::
:::::

For the last part of the exercise we let $k$ be defined as in (c).

(d) Show that $\phi$ has at least five different zeros in $[a,b]$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Since $\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx=\int_a^m\phi(x)\,dx=0$, we must have that $\int_m^b\phi(x)\,dx=0$.
Since $\phi$ is continuous, there is a $u\in(a,m)$ so that $\phi(u)=0$, and a $v\in(m,b)$ so that $\phi(v)=0$.
$\phi$ therefore has at least five different zeros in $[a,b]$, since we also proved that $\phi(a)=\phi(m)=\phi(b)=0$.
:::::::
:::::

(e) Rolles theorem says that, for a continuous, differentiable function defined on $[a,b]$ so that $\phi(a)=\phi(b)=0$, there exists a point $c\in(a,b)$ so that $\phi'(c)=0$.
Use Rolles theorem to show that there exists a $\xi\in(a,b)$ so that $\phi^{(4)}(\xi)=0$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
You an argument as follows

1. If you apply Rolles theorem on the four intervals $(a,u)$, $(u,m)$, $(m,v)$, and $(v,b)$, we get four points
$a_1<a_2<a_3<a_4$, where all $\phi'(a_i)=0$.
2. If you apply Rolles teorem again, but now on the three inetrvals $(a_1,a_2)$, $(a_2,a_3)$, and $(a_3,a_4)$, we get three points
$b_1<b_2<b_3$, where all $\phi''(b_i)=0$.
3. If you apply Rolles teorem a third time, now on the two intervals $(b_1,b_2)$, $(b_2,b_3)$, we get two points
$c_1<c_2$ so that $\phi'''(c_1)=\phi'''(c_2)=0$.
4. If you apply Rolles teorem a fourth and final time we get a $\xi\in(c_1,c_2)$ so that $\phi^{(4)}(\xi)=0$,

:::::::
:::::

(f) Explain that, with $\xi$ as in (e), we get that $E=-f^{(4)}(\xi)(b-a)^5/2880$.
It follows that the error for one interval is $\leq M_4(b-a)^5/2880$. 
Since we have contribution from $n$ such, we get the upper bound
$$nM_4(2h)^5/2880 = (b-a)M_4(2h)^4/2880 = M_4(b-a)h^4/180$$
for the error. This is considerably better than the global error estimate given in @eq-simpglobalerr.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Evaluation of @eq-phi4der in $\xi$ gives
$$0 =  f^{(4)}(\xi) + 120\frac{4!E}{(b-a)^5},$$
so that $E=-f^{(4)}(\xi)(b-a)^5/2880$. An upper bound for the error on one interval is therefore $M_4(b-a)^5/2880$.
:::::::
:::::
:::

::: {#exr-simpson}

(a) Show that the Newton form of the polynomial interpolating $f$ in $a$, $m=(a+b)/2$, and $b$ is
$$p_2(x)=f(a) + \frac{f(m)-f(a)}{h}(x-a) + \frac{f(a) - 2f(m)+f(b)}{2h^2}(x-a)(x-m),$$
where $h=(b-a)/2$.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
The Newton form is obtained by solving the equations
\begin{align*}
f(a)  &= c_0 \\
f(m) &= c_0 + c_1h \\
f(b)  &= c_0 + 2c_1h + 2c_2h^2.
\end{align*}
We get $c_0=f(a)$, $c_1=\frac{f(m)-f(a)}{h}$, $c_2=\frac{f(a)-2f(m)+f(b)}{2h^2}$. The interpolating polynomial is thus
$$
p_2(x)=f(a) + \frac{f(m)-f(a)}{h}(x-a) + \frac{f(a) - 2f(m)+f(b)}{2h^2}(x-a)(x-m).
$$
:::::::
:::::

(b) Show that $\int_a^b p_2(x)\,dx=\frac{h}{3}  \left(  f(a) + 4f(m) + f(b) \right)$.

::::: {.callout-tip title='Hint' collapse="true"}
Compute $\int_a^b (x-a)(x-m)\,dx$ first, see @exr-regnutQn. 
:::::

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
Here it can be of help to first compute $\int_a^b (x-a)(x-m)\,dx$ by means of integration by parts:
$$
\int_a^b (x-a)(x-m)\,dx 
= [\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^2(x-m)]_a^b - \frac{1}{2}\int_a^b (x-a)^2\,dx
= 2h^3 - \frac{4}{3}h^3 = \frac{2}{3}h^3.
$$
Integrating $p_2(x)$ gives
\begin{align*}
&\left[ f(a)(x-a) + \frac{f(m)-f(a)}{2h}(x-a)^2  \right]_a^b  + \frac{f(a)-2f(m)+f(b)}{2h^2}\frac{2}{3}h^3 \\
&= 2f(a)h + 2(f(m)-f(a))h  + \frac{f(a)-2f(m)+f(b)}{h}\frac{1}{3}h \\
&= h\left( 2f(m) + \frac{1}{3}(f(a)-2f(m)+f(b)) \right) \\
&= \frac{h}{3}  \left(  6f(m) + f(a)-2f(m)+f(b) \right) \\
&= \frac{h}{3}  \left(  f(a) + 4f(m) + f(b) \right).
\end{align*}
:::::::
:::::
:::





::: {#exr-}
On the interval $[x_{i-1},x_i]$ the trapezoidal rule uses only the function values $f(x_{i-1})$ and $f(x_i)$. 
On the next interval the function values $f(x_i)$ and $f(x_{i+1})$ are used. All function values, except the first and last, therefore occur twice in the sum to the right in @eq-trapezoid0.
Function evaluations can be costly - they can for example stem from sensors which are expensive to use.
Rewrite @eq-trapezoid0 in such a way that we repeat repeating function evaluations.

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
We can rewrite this as follows.
$$I_\text{trap}(h)=h\Biggl(\frac{f(a)+f(b)}{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f(x_i)\Biggr).$$
:::::::
:::::
:::



::: {#exr-}
Suppose we know  $n+1$ function values $\{f(a+kh)\}_{k=0}^n$. Show that
$$
\int_a^{a+nh} p_n(x)\,dx 
=
hn\left( f(a) + \begin{pmatrix} \frac{n}{2} & \frac{n^2}{3} & \cdots & \frac{n^n}{n+1}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} h^1p_n^{(1)}(a)/1!  \\ h^2p_n^{(2)}(a)/2! \\ \vdots \\ h^np_n^{(n)}(a)/n!\end{pmatrix} \right)
$$
Also show that, for $n=2$ and $n=3$, we get in particular 
\begin{align*}
\int_a^{a+2h} p_n(x)\,dx &= \frac{h}{3}( f(a)+4f(a+h)+f(a+2h)) \\
\int_a^{a+3h} p_n(x)\,dx &= \frac{3h}{8}( f(a)+3f(a+h)+3f(a+2h)+f(a+3h) ).
\end{align*}

::::: {.callout-tip title='Hint' collapse="true"}
@thm-derivert-approksimasjon gives us an expression for 
$\begin{pmatrix} h^1p_n^{(1)}(a)/1!  \\ h^2p_n^{(2)}(a)/2! \\ \vdots \\ h^np_n^{(n)}(a)/n!\end{pmatrix}$.
:::::

::::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::::::: {.callout-important title='Solution' collapse="true"}
We have that
\begin{align*}
\int_a^{a+nh} p_n(x)\,dx  &= \int_a^{a+nh} \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{p_n^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k\,dx = \left[ \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{p_n^{(k)}(a)}{(k+1)!}(x-a)^{k+1} \right]_a^{a+nh} \\
&= \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{p_n^{(k)}(a)}{(k+1)!}(nh)^{k+1} \\
&= 
hn\left( f(a) + \begin{pmatrix} \frac{n}{2} & \frac{n^2}{3} & \cdots & \frac{n^n}{n+1}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} h^1p_n^{(1)}(a)/1!  \\ h^2p_n^{(2)}(a)/2! \\ \vdots \\ h^np_n^{(n)}(a)/n!\end{pmatrix} \right)
\end{align*}
which is the expression we wanted. For $n=2$ @thm-derivert-approksimasjon gives
$$
\begin{pmatrix} h^1p_2^{(1)}(a)/1!  \\ h^2p_2^{(2)}(a)/2! \end{pmatrix} 
= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}f(a+h)-f(a) \\ f(a+2h) - f(a)\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1/2 \\ -1 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}f(a+h)-f(a) \\ f(a+2h) - f(a)\end{pmatrix}
$$
Inserting this is the expression above we get
\begin{align*}
&2h\left( f(a) + \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \frac{4}{3} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1/2 \\ -1 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}f(a+h)-f(a) \\ f(a+2h) - f(a)\end{pmatrix} \right) \\
&= 2h\left( f(a) + \begin{pmatrix} \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{6} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}f(a+h)-f(a) \\ f(a+2h) - f(a)\end{pmatrix}  \right) \\
&= 2h\left( \left(1-\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{6}\right)f(a) + \frac{2}{3}f(a+h) + \frac{1}{6}f(a+2h) \right) \\
&= \frac{h}{3}(f(a)+4f(a+h)+f(a+2h)).
\end{align*}
For $n=3$ @thm-derivert-approksimasjon gives
\begin{align*}
\begin{pmatrix} h^1p_3^{(1)}(a)/1!  \\ h^2p_3^{(2)}(a)/2! \\ h^3p_3^{(3)}(a)/3!\end{pmatrix} 
&= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 2 & 4 & 8 \\ 3 & 9 & 27\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}f(a+h)-f(a) \\ f(a+2h) - f(a) \\ f(a+3h) - f(a) \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 3   & -3/2 &   1/3 \\ -5/2  &  2   & -1/2 \\ 1/2   & -1/2 &  1/6 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}f(a+h)-f(a) \\ f(a+2h) - f(a) \\ f(a+3h) - f(a) \end{pmatrix}
\end{align*}
Inserting this is the expression we get
\begin{align*} 
&3h\left( f(a) + \begin{pmatrix} \frac{3}{2} & 3 & \frac{27}{4} \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 3   & -3/2 &   1/3 \\ -5/2  &  2   & -1/2\\ 1/2  & -1/2  &  1/6\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}f(a+h)-f(a) \\ f(a+2h) - f(a) \\ f(a+3h)-f(a) \end{pmatrix}\right) \\
&=  3h\left(f(a) + \begin{pmatrix} \frac{3}{8}    & \frac{3}{8} &  \frac{1}{8} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}f(a+h)-f(a) \\ f(a+2h) - f(a) \\ f(a+3h)-f(a) \end{pmatrix}\right) \\
&= 3h\left( \left((1-\frac{3}{8}-\frac{3}{8}-\frac{1}{8}\right)f(a) + \frac{3}{8}f(a+h) + \frac{3}{8} f(a+2h) + \frac{1}{8}f(a+3h) \right) \\
&= \frac{3h}{8}(f(a)+3f(a+h)+3f(a+2h)+f(a+3h)).
\end{align*}
:::::::
:::::
:::
